passage: At 7 p.m. in the Whitefield office, Mridul was filling in the travel claim from the Hyderabad trip. The client dinner had cost 1,800, but his own dinner the night before, 900, had no receipt and wasn't claimable. He hovered over the form. People in sales claimed taxi rides they never took; everyone knew it. A dinner was nothing. Then he pictured Sumit, who sat across from him and trusted his numbers on every shared project, scrolling through this claim. Would he be fine with Sumit reading line four? He deleted the line. When Sumit leaned over and asked, "Heading out?", Mridul said, "Yeah. Just finished the claim," and felt oddly light walking to the lift.

qa.q: Which dinner had no receipt?
qa.a: His own dinner the night before, 900, had no receipt.

qa.q: Why did adding the dinner feel almost acceptable to Mridul at first?
qa.a: At first Mridul felt at ease, comparing it with people in sales claiming taxi rides they never took, so one dinner seemed like nothing.

qa.q: What question helped Mridul decide, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked whether he'd be fine with Sumit reading line four, which measured the claim by his own standard instead of by what others get away with.

qa.q: How might Sumit's trust be affected if the dinner had stayed in?
qa.a: Sumit relies on Mridul's numbers on every shared project; a padded claim, even unseen, would make that trust less deserved.

grounding: An office worker resists padding an expense claim by imagining a trusted colleague reading it.

passage:
'Mumma, what's that?' Minakshi asked, climbing onto the chair beside the laptop, crayon still in hand.
'My office expense form, baby. The money I spent on work.'
Sharmila's husband Deepak called from the sofa, 'Add the Pune hotel upgrade too. Your manager won't check. Everyone in your office pads a bit.'
'The upgrade was for me, not for work,' Sharmila said.
'So? Others claim whole family trips.'
Minakshi pointed at the screen. 'Can I read it? I know my numbers!'
Sharmila looked at the little finger on the screen. 'Would I read this line out to her?' she said softly.
'What?' said Deepak.
'Nothing. Just, no. If Minakshi can read it out loud and I don't wince, it goes in. The upgrade stays out.'
She deleted the line. 'Now you can read, baby.'

qa.q: What did Deepak tell Sharmila to add to the form?
qa.a: He told her to add the Pune hotel upgrade too.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking when she looked at Minakshi's finger on the screen?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and was wondering whether she could read the upgrade line out to her daughter without wincing, a quiet check against her own standard.

qa.q: What rule did Sharmila choose, and why is it hard to argue with?
qa.a: Anything Minakshi can read out loud without Sharmila wincing goes in; it measures the form by her own values, not by the family trips others claim.

qa.q: Why might Deepak see the upgrade differently from Sharmila?
qa.a: Deepak measures it against what others in the office get away with, so padding a bit looks normal to him, while Sharmila measures it against herself.

grounding: A mother tempted to pad an expense form asks whether she would be comfortable with her child reading it.

passage: I'm Tanvir, and last quarter I almost did something small and stupid. I'd lost the receipt for a site-visit lunch in Nashik, and the claim form let me type any amount. My team lead once told me, laughing, that someone in finance had claimed a whole wedding as "client entertainment." Next to that, rounding my lunch up to 1,200 felt like a rounding error. My cursor sat there for a while. Then I thought of Damini, who has worked beside me for two years and double-checks my reports because she knows I hate mistakes. If she opened this form, would I want to explain that number? I typed the real amount, 640, and attached a note about the lost receipt. Honestly, it felt better than the extra money would have.

qa.q: What amount did Tanvir finally type?
qa.a: The real amount, 640, with a note about the lost receipt.

qa.q: Why did rounding up to 1,200 feel like a rounding error to Tanvir at first?
qa.a: Tanvir felt tempted but not guilty, because beside the story of someone claiming a whole wedding, a padded lunch looked tiny and didn't feel like real dishonesty.

qa.q: Which question changed Tanvir's decision, and why does it work?
qa.a: Imagining Damini opening the form and asking "would I want to explain that number?" works because it uses a trusted person's eyes, not the worst example.

qa.q: How might Damini feel if she found a padded number in Tanvir's form?
qa.a: Damini, who double-checks Tanvir's reports out of care, might feel let down and start wondering what else needs checking.

grounding: The narrator avoids inflating a lunch claim by imagining a trusted colleague reading it.

passage:
Mentor's note, finance team, Gangtok office. Dolma.
Anirban (25, sales) came to my desk at 6 p.m. with his claim for the Siliguri trip. He said, a bit embarrassed, that he had almost added a dinner that never happened, 'about eight hundred, the kind of thing everyone adds'.
What stopped him, he said, was a question he'd started asking himself: would I be fine if Pemba saw this? Pemba shares his desk and trained him, and he couldn't picture handing Pemba that line.
The claim he gave me had real receipts only, and one taxi fare marked 'no receipt, driver had no printer', which I appreciated.
Next step: I've asked him to share his 'would Pemba be fine' question at Friday's new-joiner session. People often need a face to check against more than another rule.

qa.a: About eight hundred.

passage:
Thursday night
Conference claims are due tomorrow. The hotel bill says two nights; I stayed one because I came back early for Irawati's fever. The front desk printed the full booking anyway. Nobody in accounts would ever check. Two people on my team openly say they pad their mileage every month, and one senior manager apparently put a family holiday down as a client visit. Compared with that, one extra night is nothing.
I had the form half filled, 'Sarika Rawat, 2 nights', when Irawati padded in with her blanket asking for water. She saw the laptop and said, 'Mumma doing homework?'
Yes, baby. And I wouldn't want you to see this homework.
Changed it to one night. Attached a note explaining the early checkout.
Slept better than I thought I would.

qa.q: Why did Sarika stay only one night at the hotel?
qa.a: Sarika came back early for Irawati's fever.

qa.q: Why did claiming the extra night feel like 'nothing' to Sarika at first?
qa.a: Sarika felt comfortable at first because, against teammates padding mileage and a senior manager's holiday booked as a client visit, one extra night looked tiny and nobody would check.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Sarika choose?
qa.a: Irawati walking in and asking about 'homework'; Sarika realised she would not want her daughter to see it, changed the claim to one night and attached a note.

qa.q: Why might the teammates who pad their mileage see Sarika's choice differently?
qa.a: To them it might look fussy or like a wasted chance, since they measure by what others get away with; Sarika is measuring by what she could show her daughter.

passage: At the end of the month, Omkar sat on the veranda of his house in Sangamner with the fuel claim form for his field visits. He had actually ridden 410 kilometres to the villages. The senior officer claimed double every month; everyone at the cooperative knew. Omkar's pen hovered over the box. A few hundred more wouldn't even be noticed. Then his four-year-old daughter Rekha climbed into his lap and pointed at the form. 'Baba, what's that?' 'A paper for the office.' 'Are you writing true things?' she asked, because that was what he always asked her about her drawings. Omkar laughed. Then he stopped laughing. If she could read this one day, would he be comfortable? He wrote 410, signed it, and let her draw a small sun in the corner of the envelope.

qa.q: How many kilometres had Omkar actually ridden?
qa.a: He had actually ridden 410 kilometres.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel when Rekha asked 'Are you writing true things?'
qa.a: He felt a jolt of uncomfortable recognition, since it was his own question to her, and it made him measure the claim against his own standard.

qa.q: Why is imagining his child reading the form a good test?
qa.a: It replaces 'the senior officer claims double' with the standard Omkar wants to live by, which resists the slide into fudging.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha one day read the form?
qa.a: She would see her Baba wrote the true figure, matching what he teaches her about telling the truth.

passage: Omar's expense report was due at midnight, and the hotel room in Toronto was quiet except for the heating. The client dinner on Tuesday was legitimate. The steak dinner alone on Wednesday, after a long day, was not. It would be so easy to write 'client follow-up'. Half the travelling team did it; he'd heard people joke about it at the airport. He typed it in. Then he thought of Wei, who sat across from him at the office, who had once driven back forty minutes to return an extra charger to a client. Omar imagined turning his screen toward Wei and saying, this one too. His face grew warm just picturing it. He deleted the line and paid for Wednesday himself. He sent the report at 11:48 and went to bed feeling oddly light.

qa.a: It was due at midnight.

qa.q: Why did Omar's face grow warm?
qa.a: Imagining Wei seeing the false entry made Omar feel embarrassed, showing the claim didn't meet the standard he respects.

qa.q: Why was picturing Wei a good countermeasure?

qa.q: How might Wei feel if told about the deleted line?
qa.a: Wei would likely feel respect for Omar's choice, since it matches the honesty Wei shows with clients.

passage:
Subject: Something small I almost did

Nandini,

You once told me, in my first week, “Write every claim as if your best friend were auditing it.” I laughed. This week I understood it.

After the Chennai trip, I had a hotel bill and a lunch bill, both genuine. I also had a personal cab to my aunt's place. The form had a line called “local conveyance.” Everyone on the floor says the big bosses fly business class on the company and call it “client travel.” Next to that, a cab felt like nothing.

I typed it in. Then I thought of you opening my form. I felt my face go hot, and I deleted the line.

Silly, maybe. But it's the first time I've noticed how easily “others do worse” pulls me along.

Thank you for that first-week advice. It actually works.

Deepika

qa.a: Deepika almost claimed a personal cab to an aunt's place as local conveyance.

qa.a: Deepika felt embarrassed imagining Nandini opening the form, which made the fudge feel real rather than minor.

qa.q: Why did imagining Nandini work better than thinking about the bosses?
qa.a: It measured the claim against a personal standard Deepika respects, instead of the worst behaviour on the floor.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel reading this email?

passage:
You asked if I've ever been tempted to fudge anything at work, Payal. Honestly? Last month.
I'm Simran, I've been at the agency two years. After the Goa shoot, I had a stack of receipts. Taxis, meals, one dinner that was really just me and my sister. And I thought, the partners claim spa weekends as “offsites.” My dinner's peanuts.
I had it on the form. Then, I don't know why, I thought of my little niece, the one who copies everything I do. I imagined her reading it over my shoulder, asking, “What's this one, Simmi?”
And I couldn't say “work.” So I took it off.
It sounds so small. But I realised I'd been letting the worst person in the building set my rules. Now I use my niece. She's a tougher auditor than finance.

passage: I'm Kalyani, and I sit beside Zubin at the travel company. Last Friday, he was filling in his expense report for the Jaipur trip. I saw him paste in two taxi receipts, then pause. The second one was from a family dinner on the same night. He looked at it for a long time. "Everyone rounds up a bit," he said, half to me. "The sales team claims whole weekends." Then he stopped. He turned his screen towards me. "Kalyani, if you saw this receipt in my report, what would you think of me?" I didn't know what to say. He answered himself. "You'd think I was a bit of a cheat. And I'd know you were right." He deleted the dinner receipt and submitted the rest. I don't know what else went on in his head. But after that he seemed lighter, humming as he packed up.

passage:
Monday. After the client meeting in Pune, Rekha and two friends had dinner at a nice restaurant. Nothing to do with work. On the train home, she opened the expense app. The bill was right there. "Client dinner," she typed. Her finger hovered. Everyone claimed dinners. Her old manager had claimed a whole holiday.
Tuesday. The draft sat in the app. Rekha kept thinking of Indu, her closest colleague, who always double-checked every rupee on her own reports. What if Indu saw this line? Rekha imagined Indu's face reading "Client dinner". Not angry. Just quietly surprised.
Wednesday. Rekha deleted the line. She submitted only the train tickets and the client lunch. At tea, Indu said, "You look happy today." Rekha laughed. "I just did something boring and honest." She didn't explain, and Indu didn't ask.

passage: Nikita, you're asking how I stayed straight in forty years of office work? Let your Hansa Ajji tell you. When I was twenty-five, I worked in the accounts section of a textile mill in Solapur. After a work trip to Mumbai, I sat with my expense sheet. My hotel was cheaper than expected. I could have written the higher amount and kept the difference. Everyone did. My supervisor claimed taxis he never took. I picked up my pen to write the bigger number. Then I thought of your mother, who was three then, sleeping at home. I asked myself, "Would I be comfortable if she grew up and saw this sheet?" The answer was no. So I wrote the true amount. It was only a small sum. But after that, I asked myself the same question every time. Not "what do the others do?", but "what would she see?"

qa.q: Where did Hansa work at twenty-five?
qa.a: In the accounts section of a textile mill in Solapur.

qa.q: How did young Hansa feel picking up the pen to write the bigger number?
qa.a: She felt tempted and uneasy, because everyone did it but it didn't sit right with her.

qa.q: What turning point in the story kept Hansa honest?
qa.a: Asking whether she'd be comfortable if her daughter saw the sheet, and making that her own standard every time.

qa.q: What might Hansa's supervisor have thought if he knew she wrote the true amount?
qa.a: He might have been surprised or thought her naive, since he claimed taxis he never took.

passage:
It was 11:50 pm, ten minutes before the finance portal closed for the month, and the hotel Wi-Fi kept dropping. Kishore's expense claim for the Nagpur trip was short: two lunches had no receipts. His teammate had said everyone just adds a "client dinner" to round it off.
He typed the line: Client dinner, ₹1,800. The cursor blinked.
He thought of Irawati, three years old and asleep at home, and pictured her reading this line one day. Then he pictured Deshpande, the colleague he trusted most, looking over his shoulder.
Would he be comfortable?
No.
He deleted it, submitted the claim as it was, and wrote to finance: "Two meals without receipts. Can I add them with a written declaration?" The portal closed at 11:59. He shut the laptop, feeling oddly light.

qa.a: The claim would look complete, but a fake dinner would sit in the records for Kishore to keep defending, and the next shortcut would feel smaller.
